{{Short description|Japanese condensed matter physicist}}
'''Kazumi Maki''' ([[kanji]]: 真木 和美,<ref>真木和美. [https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/39217731.pdf "The Magnetic Properties of Superconducting Alloys III: Abrikosov Structure (2)."] 物性研究 2, no. 3 (1964): 111-118.</ref> [[kana]]: まき かずみ ''Maki Kazumi'', January 27, 1936, [[Takamatsu, Japan]] – September 10, 2008, Los Angeles) was a Japanese theoretical physicist, known for his research in "[[superconductivity]], [[superfluid]] [[Helium-3|³He]], and quasi‑one‑dimensional (1D) materials."<ref name=obitPT>{{cite journal|author=Haas, Stephan|author2=Baeriswyl, Dionys|author3=Vollhardt, Dieter|url=https://opus.bibliothek.uni-augsburg.de/opus4/files/93513/93513.pdf|doi=10.1063/PT.4.2036 |title=Obituary of Kazumi Maki |journal=Physics Today |year=2009 |issue=4 }}</ref>
 
==Biography==
Kazumi Maki spent most of his childhood in Kyoto.<ref name=obitPT/> During WW II he with his family moved to a rural area because of a scarcity of food and the danger of aerial attack.<ref name=obitUSC>{{cite journal|author=Johnson, Pamela|date=September 1, 2008|url=https://dornsife.usc.edu/news/stories/335/in-memoriam-kazumi-maki-72/|title=In Memoriam: Kazumi Maki, 72|publisher=University of Southern California}}</ref> At [[Kyoto University]] he received his Ph.D. in 1964 with a thesis on theoretical particle physics, written under the supervision of [[Hideki Yukawa]]. Maki was a postdoc at the [[University of Chicago]] for the academic year 1964–1965 and an assistant professor from 1965 to 1967 at the [[University of California, San Diego]]. From 1967 to 1974 he was a professor at 
[[Tohoku University]]. From 1974 until his death in 2008 he was a professor at the [[University of Southern California]] (USC).<ref name=obitPT/> For the academic year 1979–1980 he was a [[Guggenheim Fellow]];<ref>{{cite web|title=Kazumi Maki|website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/kazumi-maki/}}</ref> during this time he worked with [[Hagen Kleinert]].

Maki was the author or co-author of approximately 500 scientific publications. In the 1960s and early 1970s his research dealt with [[BCS theory]]. In 1968 he published his theoretical analysis predicting an anomalous increase in electrical conductivity caused by superconducting fluctuations just above the [[Superconductivity#By critical temperature|critical temperature for a low-temperature superconductor]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Critical Fluctuation of the Order Parameter in a Superconductor. I|author=Maki, Kazumi|journal=Progress of Theoretical Physics|volume=40|issue=2|date=August 1968|pages=193–200|doi=10.1143/PTP.40.193|bibcode=1968PThPh..40..193M |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Thompson, Richard S.|title=Microwave, flux flow, and fluctuation resistance of dirty type-II superconductors|journal=Physical Review B|volume=1|issue=1|date=January 1970|pages=327–333|doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.1.327|bibcode=1970PhRvB...1..327T }}</ref> This predicted increase in conductivity is empirically valid, and the corresponding term in perturbation theory is now called the "Maki-Thompson term."<ref name=obitPT/> Maki also did research on pair breaking of Cooper pairs and the accompanying gapless (zero gap) superconductivity, in which there is ''s''-wave superconductivity in the presence of impurities, causing a range of temperatures where the [[energy gap]] vanishes.<ref>{{cite book|author=Abrikosov, A. A.|chapter=Chapter 21. Superconductivity and magnetism|title=Fundamentals of the Theory of Metals|date=18 October 2017 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tTo2DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA511|page=511|isbn=9780486819013|publisher=Dover}} (reprint of 1988 North-Holland original)</ref><ref name=obitPT/> He contributed an important review paper<ref name=obitPT/> ''Gapless Superconductivity'' to volume 2 of the classic 2-volume ''Superconductivity'' edited by Ronald D. Parks<ref>{{cite journal|author=Guertin, R.P.|author2=Denboer, M.|author3=Williamson, S.J.|year=1986|title=Obituary. Ronald D. Parks|journal=Physics Today|volume=39|issue=6|page=111|doi=10.1063/1.2815062|bibcode=1986PhT....39f.111G|doi-access=free}}</ref> and published by [[Marcel Dekker]] in 1969.

From the early 1970s until 1990, Maki investigated superfluid ³He and quasi-one-dimensional materials.<ref name=obitPT/>

From 1991 until the end of his life, he worked on [[high-temperature superconductors]] and investigated the effects of anisotropic ordering parameters on the transport and magnetic properties both in the superconducting state and in the pseudo-gap phase. He saw the pseudo-gap phase as a kind of unconventional spin-density wave. As evidence accumulated for ''d''-wave pairing in high-temperature copper oxide superconductors, he pointed out the much greater susceptibility of ''d''-waves to pair breakage from non-magnetic impurities because, unlike conventional ''s''-wave superconductivity, they have topologically protected nodes. He pursued the idea of ''gossamer superconductivity'' (''d''-wave superconductivity in the presence of ''d''-density waves) and half-integer flux quanta in unconventional superconductors.<ref name=obitPT/>

Kazumi Maki was elected in 1981 a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1981&unit_id=&institution=University+of+Southern+California}} (search on year=1981 and institution=University of Southern California)</ref> He received in 1972 the [[Nishina Memorial Prize]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Faculty Honors|website=Physics & Astronomy, University of Southern California|url=https://physics.usc.edu/Faculty/Prizes.html|access-date=2022-09-27|archive-date=2022-07-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220714153010/https://physics.usc.edu/Faculty/Prizes.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> and in 2006, from the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]] (UIUC), the {{ill|John Bardeen Prize|de}} with citation "for his work on gapless quasiparticle excitations due to pair-breaking and for elucidating the role of fluctuations".<ref>{{cite web|title=John Bardeen Prize Winners|website=Physics, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign|url=https://physics.illinois.edu/people/honors-and-awards/bardeen-prize}}</ref>

His doctoral students include [[Robijn Bruinsma]] and [[Dieter Vollhardt]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Kazumi Maki|website=Physics Tree|url=https://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=187254}}</ref>

He and his wife, Masako, were aficionados of the [[Los Angeles Music Center]]. At their home they frequently played duets — Kazumi's violin and Masako's piano. Upon his death he was survived by his widow.<ref name=obitUSC/>
